idiom_name: class for the concept, module for namespacing and stateless behaviour, Data for value concepts
implementation_notes: Ruby's class is the concept home - state, methods and invariants - while modules carry the two things a class is bad at: namespacing a package of related behaviour and mixing a shared role into several classes, and Data.define models an immutable value concept. The pattern's Ruby form is therefore an explicit choice: identity and state imply a class, stateless cohesive operations a module (often extend self or module_function), a value a Data object, a shared role a mixin. Because classes and modules can be reopened, the same concept is easily re-scattered by patches, so keep each concept's methods in the file that defines it.
pitfalls: Reopening classes and modules (or gems that do) scatters a concept across files and makes method resolution order-dependent; confine patches and prefer explicit modules you own.
include/extend mixins resolve last-in-first-wins, so two mixins can silently shadow the concept's own methods.
A class whose methods are all class methods (self.foo) is a module pretending to be a class; extend self states 'no instances' honestly.
